claim: Reproductive division of labor (e.g. germ-soma specialization) is a hallmark of the evolution of multicellularity.
source: Reproductive division of labor (e.g. germ-soma specialization) is a hallmark of the evolution of multicellularity, signifying the emergence of a new type of individual and facilitating the evolution of increased organismal complexity.
evidence: This is a statement about the significance of reproductive division of labor in evolutionary biology, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Reproductive division of labor signifies the emergence of a new type of individual.
source: Reproductive division of labor (e.g. germ-soma specialization) is a hallmark of the evolution of multicellularity, signifying the emergence of a new type of individual and facilitating the evolution of increased organismal complexity.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the evolutionary significance of reproductive division of labor, based on established knowledge.

claim: Reproductive division of labor facilitates the evolution of increased organismal complexity.
source: Reproductive division of labor (e.g. germ-soma specialization) is a hallmark of the evolution of multicellularity, signifying the emergence of a new type of individual and facilitating the evolution of increased organismal complexity.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the evolutionary consequences of reproductive division of labor, based on established knowledge.

claim: Classical models predict that specialization is beneficial when further division of labor produces an accelerating increase in absolute productivity.
source: A large body of work from evolutionary biology, economics, and ecology has shown that specialization is beneficial when further division of labor produces an accelerating increase in absolute productivity (i.e. productivity is a convex function of specialization).
evidence: This claim is supported by references to prior work in multiple fields.

claim: Reproductive specialization can evolve even when the benefits of specialization are saturating (i.e. productivity is a concave function of specialization).
source: Here we show that reproductive specialization is qualitatively different from classical models of resource sharing, and can evolve even when the benefits of specialization are saturating (i.e. productivity is a concave function of specialization).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by analytical theory and simulations presented in the paper.

claim: Reproductive specialization is strongly favored in sparse networks of cellular interactions that reflect the morphology of early, simple multicellular organisms.
source: Through analytical theory and evolutionary individual-based simulations, we demonstrate that reproductive specialization is strongly favored in sparse networks of cellular interactions that reflect the morphology of early, simple multicellular organisms, highlighting the importance of restricted social interactions in the evolution of reproductive specialization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by analytical theory and simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The evolution of multicellularity set the stage for unprecedented increases in organismal complexity.
source: The evolution of multicellularity set the stage for unprecedented increases in organismal complexity (Szathmáry and Smith, 1995; Knoll, 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A key factor in the success of multicellular strategies is the ability to take advantage of within-organism specialization through cellular differentiation.
source: A key factor in the remarkable success of multicellular strategies is the ability to take advantage of within-organism specialization through cellular differentiation (Queller and Strassmann, 2009; Brunet and King, 2017; Cavalier-Smith, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Reproductive specialization includes both the creation of a specialized germ line during ontogeny (as in animals and volvocine green algae) and functional differentiation into reproductive and non-reproductive tissues (as in plants, green and red macroalgae, and fungi).
source: Reproductive specialization, which includes both the creation of a specialized germ line during ontogeny (as in animals and volvocine green algae) and functional differentiation into reproductive and non-reproductive tissues (as in plants, green and red macroalgae, and fungi), may be especially important (Cooper and West, 2018; Michod et al., 2006; Ispolatov et al., 2012; Solari et al., 2013; Michod, 2007; West et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations and established biological knowledge.

claim: Reproductive specialization is an unambiguous indication that biological individuality rests firmly at the level of the multicellular organism.
source: Reproductive specialization is an unambiguous indication that biological individuality rests firmly at the level of the multicellular organism (Michod, 1999; Folse and Roughgarden, 2010), and is thought to play an important role in spurring the evolution of further complexity by inhibiting within-organism (cell-level) evolution (Buss, 1988) and limiting reversion to unicellularity (Libby and Ratcliff, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Reproductive specialization plays an important role in spurring the evolution of further complexity by inhibiting within-organism (cell-level) evolution.
source: Reproductive specialization is an unambiguous indication that biological individuality rests firmly at the level of the multicellular organism (Michod, 1999; Folse and Roughgarden, 2010), and is thought to play an important role in spurring the evolution of further complexity by inhibiting within-organism (cell-level) evolution (Buss, 1988) and limiting reversion to unicellularity (Libby and Ratcliff, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Reproductive specialization limits reversion to unicellularity.
source: Reproductive specialization is an unambiguous indication that biological individuality rests firmly at the level of the multicellular organism (Michod, 1999; Folse and Roughgarden, 2010), and is thought to play an important role in spurring the evolution of further complexity by inhibiting within-organism (cell-level) evolution (Buss, 1988) and limiting reversion to unicellularity (Libby and Ratcliff, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The origin and further evolution of reproductive specialization during the transition to multicellularity remain poorly understood.
source: Despite the central importance of reproductive specialization, its origin and further evolution during the transition to multicellularity remain poorly understood (McShea, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: Specialization pays off only when it increases total productivity, compared to the case where each individual simply produces what they need.
source: A large body of theory from these fields shows that specialization pays off only when it increases total productivity, compared to the case where each individual simply produces what they need (Szathmáry and Smith, 1995; Smith and Szathmáry, 1997; Goldsby et al., 2012; Corning and Szathmáry, 2015; Hidalgo and Hausmann, 2009; Boza et al., 2014; Taborsky et al., 2016; Page et al., 2006; Rueffler et al., 2012; Szekely et al., 2013; Findlay, 2008; Amado et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Highly reciprocal interactions, which facilitate exchange between complementary specialists, amplify cooperation.
source: Certain types of trading arrangements maximize the benefits of specialization; highly reciprocal interactions, which facilitate exchange between complementary specialists, amplify cooperation (Allen et al., 2017; Pavlogiannis et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Previous work finds that even when groups grow in an ideal spatial arrangement, increased specialization and trade is only favored by natural selection when productivity increases as an accelerating function of the degree of specialization.
source: Still, previous work finds that even when groups grow in an ideal spatial arrangement, increased specialization and trade is only favored by natural selection when productivity increases as an accelerating function of the degree of specialization (i.e., productivity is a convex, or super-linear, function of the degree of specialization).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from prior work, as indicated by the context.

claim: Saturating functional returns (i.e. productivity is a concave, or sub-linear, function of the degree of specialization) should inhibit the evolution of specialization according to previous work.
source: Conversely, saturating functional returns (i.e. productivity is a concave, or sub-linear, function of the degree of specialization) should inhibit the evolution of specialization (Cooper and West, 2018; Michod et al., 2006; Ispolatov et al., 2012; Solari et al., 2013; Michod, 2007; West et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Trade between germ (reproductive) and somatic (non-reproductive) cells is intrinsically asymmetric, because the cooperative action, multicellular replication, is not a product that is shared evenly.
source: Trade between germ (reproductive) and somatic (non-reproductive) cells is intrinsically asymmetric, because the cooperative action, multicellular replication, is not a product that is shared evenly.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the nature of reproductive specialization, based on logical inference.

claim: Selection acts primarily on the fitness of the multicellular group as a whole.
source: Selection acts primarily on the fitness of the multicellular group as a whole (Folse and Roughgarden, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Optimal specialization can result in behaviors that reduce the short-term fitness of some cells within the multicellular group.
source: As a result, optimal specialization can result in behaviors that reduce the short-term fitness of some cells within the multicellular group (Michod et al., 2006; Michod, 2007), often manifest as reproductive altruism.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Network theory has proven to be an exceptionally powerful and versatile technique for analyzing social dynamics.
source: Network theory has proven to be an exceptionally powerful and versatile technique for analyzing social dynamics (Wey et al., 2008; Lieberman et al., 2005), and indeed, is uniquely well suited to understanding the evolution of early multicellular organisms.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When cells adhere through permanent bonds, sparse network-like bodies (i.e. filaments and trees) often result.
source: When cells adhere through permanent bonds, sparse network-like bodies (i.e. filaments and trees) often result (Amado et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: This mode of group formation is common today among simple multicellular organisms.
source: This mode of group formation is not only common today among simple multicellular organisms (Umen, 2014; Claessen et al., 2014), but is the dominant mode of group formation in the lineages evolving complex multicellularity (i.e. plants, red algae, brown algae, and fungi, but not animals).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Sparse network-like body formation is the dominant mode of group formation in the lineages evolving complex multicellularity (i.e. plants, red algae, brown algae, and fungi, but not animals).
source: This mode of group formation is not only common today among simple multicellular organisms (Umen, 2014; Claessen et al., 2014), but is the dominant mode of group formation in the lineages evolving complex multicellularity (i.e. plants, red algae, brown algae, and fungi, but not animals).
evidence: This is a statement about evolutionary patterns, based on established knowledge.

claim: Under a broad class of sparse networks, complete functional specialization can be adaptive even when returns from dividing labor are saturating (i.e. concave/sub linear).
source: We find that under a broad class of sparse networks, complete functional specialization can be adaptive even when returns from dividing labor are saturating (i.e. concave/sub linear).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by analytical theory and simulations.

claim: Sparse networks impose constraints on who can share with whom, which counterintuitively increases the benefit of specialization.
source: Sparse networks impose constraints on who can share with whom, which counterintuitively increases the benefit of specialization (McShea, 2000).
evidence: This is a finding of the manuscript, supported by analytical theory and simulations, with a citation to related prior work.

claim: By dividing labor, multicellular groups can capitalize on high between-cell variance in behavior, ultimately increasing group-level reproduction.
source: By dividing labor, multicellular groups can capitalize on high between-cell variance in behavior, ultimately increasing group-level reproduction.
evidence: This is an inference from the model and results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Group morphologies that naturally arise from simple biophysical mechanisms strongly promote reproductive specialization.
source: Further, we consider group morphologies that naturally arise from simple biophysical mechanisms and show that these morphologies strongly promote reproductive specialization.
evidence: This is a finding of the manuscript, supported by simulations and analysis.

claim: Reproductive specialization can evolve under a far broader set of conditions than previously thought.
source: Our results show that reproductive specialization can evolve under a far broader set of conditions than previously thought, lowering a key barrier to major evolutionary transitions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of the manuscript.

claim: Viability is defined as activities keeping the cell alive (e.g. investing in cellular homeostasis or behaviors that improve survival).
source: We define viability as activities keeping the cell alive (e.g. investing in cellular homeostasis or behaviors that improve survival), and fecundity as activities involved in cellular reproduction.
evidence: This is a definitional statement for the model.

claim: Fecundity is defined as activities involved in cellular reproduction.
source: We define viability as activities keeping the cell alive (e.g. investing in cellular homeostasis or behaviors that improve survival), and fecundity as activities involved in cellular reproduction.
evidence: This is a definitional statement for the model.

claim: Multicellular organisms readily evolve differentiated cells that are completely reliant on helper cells.
source: At the cellular level, there appears to be a fundamental asymmetry in how viability effort and fecundity effort can be shared among cells: while multicellular organisms readily evolve differentiated cells that are completely reliant on helper cells (i.e. glial cells that support neurons in animals or companion cells that support sieve tube cells in plants), no cell can directly share its ability to reproduce.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biological knowledge, with examples provided.

claim: No cell can directly share its ability to reproduce.
source: At the cellular level, there appears to be a fundamental asymmetry in how viability effort and fecundity effort can be shared among cells: while multicellular organisms readily evolve differentiated cells that are completely reliant on helper cells (i.e. glial cells that support neurons in animals or companion cells that support sieve tube cells in plants), no cell can directly share its ability to reproduce.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement based on biological reasoning.

claim: In the model, viability can be shared across connected cells, but fecundity cannot be shared.
source: We thus use a model in which viability can be shared across connected cells, but fecundity cannot be shared (note, in order to test the sensitivity of our predictions to this assumption, in a later section we will consider the more general case in which viability and fecundity can both be shared, but by different amounts).
evidence: This is a description of the model assumptions.

claim: Connecting alternating specialists creates a bipartite graph which maximizes the benefits of specialization and the range of parameters for which it is advantageous.
source: Connecting alternating specialists creates a bipartite graph which maximizes the benefits of specialization and the range of parameters for which it is advantageous.
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1c and analytical results.

claim: Preventing trade between most cells encourages division of labor in the neighbor network.
source: Surprisingly, preventing trade between most cells encourages division of labor.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations and analysis of the neighbor network.

claim: The neighbor network topology leads to alternating specialists in viability and fecundity.
source: In our simulations, this topology leads to alternating specialists in viability and fecundity (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Specialization evolves for a wider range of α and β values for the balanced bipartite network than for the neighbor network.
source: However, we find that specialization evolves for a wider range of α and β values for the balanced bipartite network than for the neighbor network.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing the results for different network topologies.

claim: When complete generalization is not a fitness maximum, a high degree of (or even complete) specialization typically does maximize fitness.
source: While we have not analytically shown where the fitness maximum occurs in cases where the generalist strategy becomes a saddle point, evolutionary simulations (Figure 1) suggest that when complete generalization is not a fitness maximum, a high degree of (or even complete) specialization typically does maximize fitness.
evidence: This is a finding from evolutionary simulations shown in Figure 1.

claim: Complete reproductive specialization occurs when both viability and fecundity specialists cannot survive independently.
source: This amounts to complete reproductive specialization (Cooper and West, 2018; Kirk, 2005; Michod, 2006).
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations.

claim: Saturating specialization (i.e. specialization despite a concave return function) occurs for the neighbor and balanced bipartite topologies in the evolving resource sharing model.
source: Saturating specialization (i.e. specialization despite a concave return function) still occurs for the neighbor and balanced bipartite topologies.
evidence: This is a finding from evolutionary simulations with evolving resource sharing.

claim: A sparse group topology constitutes a cooperation-prone physical substrate that can favor the evolution of cellular specialization.
source: Therefore, a sparse group topology constitutes a cooperation-prone physical substrate that can favor the evolution of cellular.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results of the manuscript.

claim: The benefit of specialization in neighbor networks increases with group size.
source: The benefit of specialization in neighbor networks increases with group size.
evidence: This is an analytical result from the mathematical analysis.

claim: Many randomly assembled graphs obtain maximum fitness through complete reproductive specialization even when α is below 1.
source: We find that many randomly assembled graphs obtain maximum fitness through complete reproductive specialization even when α is below 1 (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations of Erdős-Rényi random graphs shown in Figure 3.

claim: When network connectivity is at its minimum, the group consists solely of isolated cells that cannot interact, and under these conditions generalists are favored.
source: When network connectivity is at its minimum, the group consists solely of isolated cells that cannot interact. Under these conditions generalists are favored.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the model structure.

claim: When connectivity is small but not zero, specialization arises most readily.
source: However, when connectivity is small but not zero, specialization arises most readily.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis of random graphs with varying connectivity.

claim: The troughs in Figure 3b, where specialization occurs for the lowest values of α, occur when connectivity is just large enough so that the existence of a spanning tree is more likely than not.
source: We conjecture that the troughs in Figure 3b, where specialization occurs for the lowest values of α, occur when connectivity is just large enough so that the existence of a spanning tree is more likely than not.
evidence: This is a conjecture based on observations from Figure 3b.

claim: Filament topologies have been widely observed in independently-evolved simple multicellular organisms, from ancient fossils of early red algae to extant multicellular bacteria and algae.
source: Filament topologies have been widely observed in independently-evolved simple multicellular organisms, from ancient fossils of early red algae (Butterfield, 2000; Figure 4a) to extant multicellular bacteria (Claessen et al., 2014) and algae (Umen, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and Figure 4a.

claim: Branching multicellular phenotypes have been observed to readily evolve from baker's yeast.
source: Branching multicellular phenotypes have also been observed to readily evolve from baker's yeast (Ratcliff et al., 2015; Figure 4b), and are reminiscent of ancient fungus-like structures (Bengtson et al., 2017a) and early multicellular fossils of unknown phylogenetic position from the early Ediacaran (Droser and Gehling, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and Figure 4b.

claim: Specialization is favored in the sub-linear regime for populations of groups with filamentous and branched topologies.
source: Simulations of populations of groups with filamentous and branched topologies reveal that specialization is indeed favored in the sub-linear regime (Figure 4a and b)
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4a and b.

claim: Sub-linear specialization is never observed for fully connected topologies.
source: conversely, sub-linear specialization is never observed for fully connected topologies (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is a finding from simulations shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Simple and easily accessible routes to multicellular group formation can readily evolve in response to selection for organismal size.
source: Simple and easily accessible routes to multicellular group formation can readily evolve in response to selection for organismal size (Ratcliff et al., 2012), and this process may also strongly favor the evolution of cellular differentiation (McCarthy and Enquist, 2005; Heim et al., 2017; McClain and Boyer, 2009; Bonner, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: When all cells within groups interact (with equal interaction strength), returns on investment must be an accelerating, that is, convex, function of investment for specialization to evolve.
source: Indeed, when all cells within groups interact (with equal interaction strength), returns on investment must be an accelerating, that is, convex, function of investment for specialization to evolve (Figure 1a; Szathmáry and Smith, 1995; Smith and Szathmáry, 1997; Corning and Szathmáry, 2015; Cooper and West, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1a and citations to prior work.

claim: For a broad class of sparsely connected networks, complete specialization can evolve even when the viability and fecundity return on investment curves are saturating, that is, concave.
source: Yet for a broad class of sparsely connected networks, complete specialization can evolve even when the viability and fecundity return on investment curves are saturating, that is, concave (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the manuscript, supported by Figure 3.

claim: Jensen's inequality guarantees that for concave ROI functions generalists produce more total viability and fecundity than specialists.
source: Jensen's inequality guarantees that for concave ROI functions generalists produce more total viability and fecundity than specialists, and that for convex ROI functions specialists produce more total viability and fecundity than generalists.
evidence: This is a statement about Jensen's inequality, which is established mathematical knowledge.

claim: Jensen's inequality guarantees that for convex ROI functions specialists produce more total viability and fecundity than generalists.
source: Jensen's inequality guarantees that for concave ROI functions generalists produce more total viability and fecundity than specialists, and that for convex ROI functions specialists produce more total viability and fecundity than generalists.
evidence: This is a statement about Jensen's inequality, which is established mathematical knowledge.

claim: Jensen's inequality does not connect ROI convexity/concavity to group fitness.
source: Crucially, however, Jensen's inequality does not connect ROI convexity/concavity to group fitness.
evidence: This is a key insight from the analysis, based on mathematical reasoning.

claim: For fully connected topologies, greater absolute productivity proportionally increases group fitness, and differentiation can only evolve with accelerating benefits of specialization.
source: For fully connected topologies (i.e. Figure 4c), greater absolute productivity proportionally increases group fitness, and differentiation can only evolve with accelerating benefits of specialization.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis and simulations.

claim: For topologically structured organisms, fitness depends on how complementary specialist cells are connected.
source: This is not the case for topologically structured organisms, where fitness also depends on how complementary specialist cells are connected.
evidence: This is an inference from the model and results.

claim: The spatial arrangement of unlike specialists plays a key role in determining their productivity (and thus fitness) in metabolic cross-feeding.
source: The importance of connecting complementary specialists has long been appreciated in other contexts, such as metabolic cross-feeding, for which it has been shown that the spatial arrangement of unlike specialists plays a key role in determining their productivity (and thus fitness) (Co et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: While Jensen's inequality ensures that generalists will produce more viability and fecundity than specialists given a concave ROI function, specialization can still increase the fitness of topologically structured groups by increasing realized productivity.
source: While Jensen's inequality ensures that generalists will produce more viability and fecundity than specialists given a concave ROI function, specialization can still increase the fitness of topologically structured groups by increasing realized productivity.
evidence: This is a key insight from the analysis, reconciling Jensen's inequality with the finding that specialization can be favored with concave ROI.

claim: Networks favoring specialization readily arise as a consequence of physical processes structuring simple cellular groups.
source: Rather than being unusual, networks favoring specialization readily arise as a consequence of physical processes structuring simple cellular groups (Allen et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Septin defects during cell division create multicellular groups with simple graph structures, where cells are connected only to parents and offspring.
source: For example, septin defects during cell division create multicellular groups with simple graph structures (Figure 4a and b), where cells are connected only to parents and offspring (Bengtson et al., 2017b; Droser and Gehling, 2008; Ratcliff et al., 2012; Ratcliff et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and Figure 4a and b.

claim: If cells share resources only with physically-attached neighbors, then the physical topology of the group describes its interaction topology, and these sparse networks strongly favor reproductive specialization.
source: If cells share resources only with physically-attached neighbors, then the physical topology of the group describes its interaction topology, and these sparse networks strongly favor reproductive specialization.
evidence: This is an inference from the model and results.

claim: The primary benefit of sparsity is that sparse networks are likely to be at least somewhat bipartite.
source: Finally, we note that the primary benefit of sparsity is that sparse networks are likely to be at least somewhat bipartite.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of different network topologies.

claim: The more bipartite-like a network is, the less effort is wasted, and the easier it is for specialization to be favored.
source: The more bipartite-like a network is, the less effort is wasted, and the easier it is for specialization to be favored.
evidence: This is an inference from the analysis of bipartite networks.

claim: Complex multicellularity (large multicellular organisms with considerable cellular differentiation) has evolved in at least five eukaryotic lineages.
source: Complex multicellularity (large multicellular organisms with considerable cellular differentiation) has evolved in at least five eukaryotic lineages, once each in the animals (King, 2004), land plants (Kenrick and Crane, 1997), and brown algae (Silberfeld et al., 2010), two or three times in the red algae (Cock and Collén, 2015; Yoon et al., 2006), and 8–11 times in fungi (Nagy et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: In all cases other than animals, complex multicellular organisms form multicellular bodies via permanent cell-cell bonds, creating long-lasting highly structured cellular networks.
source: In all cases other than animals, these organisms form multicellular bodies via permanent cell-cell bonds, creating long-lasting highly structured cellular networks.
evidence: This is a statement about the biology of complex multicellular organisms, based on established knowledge.

claim: Both fossil and phylogenetic evidence suggests that early multicellular organisms in these lineages were considerably less complex, growing as relatively simple graph structures.
source: Both fossil and phylogenetic evidence suggests that early multicellular organisms in these lineages were considerably less complex, growing as relatively simple graph structures.
evidence: This is a statement about evolutionary history, based on fossil and phylogenetic evidence.

claim: 1.2 billion year old red algae formed linear filaments of cells.
source: For example, 1.2 billion year old red algae formed linear filaments of cells (Butterfield, 2000), basal multicellular charophyte algae formed circular sheets of cells radiating from a common center (Kenrick and Crane, 1997), the ancestor of the brown algae likely formed a branched haplostichous thallus that was either filamentous or pseudoparenchymatous (Silberfeld et al., 2010), and hyphal fungi are primarily composed of linear chains of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Basal multicellular charophyte algae formed circular sheets of cells radiating from a common center.
source: For example, 1.2 billion year old red algae formed linear filaments of cells (Butterfield, 2000), basal multicellular charophyte algae formed circular sheets of cells radiating from a common center (Kenrick and Crane, 1997), the ancestor of the brown algae likely formed a branched haplostichous thallus that was either filamentous or pseudoparenchymatous (Silberfeld et al., 2010), and hyphal fungi are primarily composed of linear chains of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The ancestor of the brown algae likely formed a branched haplostichous thallus that was either filamentous or pseudoparenchymatous.
source: For example, 1.2 billion year old red algae formed linear filaments of cells (Butterfield, 2000), basal multicellular charophyte algae formed circular sheets of cells radiating from a common center (Kenrick and Crane, 1997), the ancestor of the brown algae likely formed a branched haplostichous thallus that was either filamentous or pseudoparenchymatous (Silberfeld et al., 2010), and hyphal fungi are primarily composed of linear chains of cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Hyphal fungi are primarily composed of linear chains of cells.
source: For example, 1.2 billion year old red algae formed linear filaments of cells (Butterfield, 2000), basal multicellular charophyte algae formed circular sheets of cells radiating from a common center (Kenrick and Crane, 1997), the ancestor of the brown algae likely formed a branched haplostichous thallus that was either filamentous or pseudoparenchymatous (Silberfeld et al., 2010), and hyphal fungi are primarily composed of linear chains of cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the biology of hyphal fungi, based on established knowledge.

claim: One hypothesis is that early metazoans resembled extant colonial choanoflagellates.
source: One hypothesis is that early metazoans resembled extant colonial choanoflagellates (Fairclough et al., 2013), the closest-living protistan relatives of the animals (Fairclough et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Extant colony-forming choanoflagellates have evolved a variety of multicellular structures with sparse cellular topologies and permanent cell-cell bonds.
source: Extant colony-forming choanoflagellates have evolved a variety of multicellular structures with sparse cellular topologies and permanent cell-cell bonds.
evidence: This is a statement about the biology of choanoflagellates, based on established knowledge.

claim: Many choanoflagellate species form branched, tree-like structures.
source: For example, many species form branched, tree-like structures (Leadbeater, 2015), Choanoeca flexa grows as a sheet of cells (Brunet et al., 2019), and Salpingoceca rosetta can form either linear chains or rosettes in which the cells are connected via cytoplasmic bridges formed through incomplete cytokinesis (Dayel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Choanoeca flexa grows as a sheet of cells.
source: For example, many species form branched, tree-like structures (Leadbeater, 2015), Choanoeca flexa grows as a sheet of cells (Brunet et al., 2019), and Salpingoceca rosetta can form either linear chains or rosettes in which the cells are connected via cytoplasmic bridges formed through incomplete cytokinesis (Dayel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Salpingoceca rosetta can form either linear chains or rosettes in which the cells are connected via cytoplasmic bridges formed through incomplete cytokinesis.
source: For example, many species form branched, tree-like structures (Leadbeater, 2015), Choanoeca flexa grows as a sheet of cells (Brunet et al., 2019), and Salpingoceca rosetta can form either linear chains or rosettes in which the cells are connected via cytoplasmic bridges formed through incomplete cytokinesis (Dayel et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Choanoflagellate growth forms all share characteristics (i.e. permanent cellular bonds and sparse topologies) that promote the evolution of cellular differentiation.
source: While these growth forms are quite diverse, they all share characteristics (i.e. permanent cellular bonds and sparse topologies) that promote the evolution of cellular differentiation.
evidence: This is an inference from the results of the manuscript applied to choanoflagellate biology.

claim: The main differences between this work and previous investigations of the effect of group topology on specialization is that this work considers the productivity of groups as a whole, not the cells within them, and considers situations of highly asymmetric sharing.
source: The main differences between our work and previous investigations of the effect of group topology on specialization is that we consider the productivity of groups as a whole, not the cells within them, and we consider situations of highly asymmetric sharing.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the approach in this manuscript.

claim: The approach in this work is general, and can be applied to other systems of trade and specialization, so long as (1) only the aggregate productivity of the group (and not the particles within it) is maximized, (2) the productivity of each particle within the group is a multiplicative function of returns on investment into two (or more) tasks, and (3) there is an asymmetry in how products of those investments are shared.
source: Our approach is general, and can be applied to other systems of trade and specialization, so long as (1) only the aggregate productivity of the group (and not the particles within it) is maximized, (2) the productivity of each particle within the group is a multiplicative function of returns on investment into two (or more) tasks, and (3) there is an asymmetry in how products of those investments are shared.
evidence: This is a statement about the generalizability of the approach.

claim: As long as sharing of two goods is sufficiently asymmetric, specialization with saturating returns on investment can still be adaptive.
source: While in this work we have focused on reproductive division of labor, a process in which fecundity returns are not shared at all, we show in the supplement that as long as sharing of two goods is sufficiently asymmetric, specialization with saturating returns on investment can still be adaptive (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: This is a finding from supplementary analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Alternative paths to specialization likely exist, such as through positional effects that result in an initially heterogeneous population of cell types.
source: Finally, we note that alternative paths to specialization likely exist. For example, cells at different positions in a group may experience different local environments, which may produce cells with varied fecundity-viability trade-offs. A previous paper demonstrated that the evolution of specialization is favored if these 'positional effects' result in an initially heterogeneous population of cell types (Tverskoi et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior work and represents speculation about alternative mechanisms.

claim: Future work examining the relationship between cellular interaction topology and cellular heterogeneity will provide unique insight into the origin and diversity of multicellular forms.
source: We thus anticipate that future work examining the relationship between cellular interaction topology and cellular heterogeneity (as well as a wide range of complex and varied relationships between viability, fecundity, and multicellular fitness) will provide unique insight into the origin and diversity of multicellular forms.
evidence: This is a speculation about future research directions.

claim: Group topological structure can play a key role in the evolution of reproductive division of labor.
source: Our results demonstrate that group topological structure can play a key role in the evolution of reproductive division of labor.

claim: Within a broad class of sparsely connected networks, specialization is favored even when the returns from cooperation are saturating (i.e. concave); this result is in direct contrast to the prevailing view that accelerating (i.e. convex), returns are required for natural selection to favor increased specialization.
source: Indeed, within a broad class of sparsely connected networks, specialization is favored even when the returns from cooperation are saturating (i.e. concave); this result is in direct contrast to the prevailing view that accelerating (i.e. convex), returns are required for natural selection to favor increased specialization (Cooper and West, 2018; Michod et al., 2006; Ispolatov et al., 2012; Solari et al., 2013; Michod, 2007; West et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the manuscript, contrasting with prior work cited.

claim: The results underscore the central importance of life history trade-offs in the origin of reproductive specialization.
source: Our results underscore the central importance of life history trade-offs in the origin of reproductive specialization (Michod et al., 2006; Michod, 2007; Hammerschmidt et al., 2014; van Gestel and Tarnita, 2017; Noh et al., 2018), and support the emerging consensus that evolutionary transitions in individuality are not necessarily highly constrained (Ratcliff et al., 2012; Ratcliff et al., 2017; Fairclough et al., 2010; Brunet and King, 2017; Pennisi, 2018; Black et al., 2019; Rose et al., 2020; van Gestel and Tarnita, 2017; Black et al., 2019; Staps et al., 2019; Grosberg and Strathmann, 2007).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results, supported by citations to prior work.
